title: Caching
summary: Put a cache on a hot read and choose invalidation before quoting hit rate.

parts.rule: Put a cache in front of a specific hot read only after defining the source-of-truth path. Name the key, value, TTL, fill policy, invalidation or refresh behavior, and acceptable staleness. Then handle misses, simultaneous expiry, and cache failure. A hit-rate estimate is useful only when it translates into reduced origin load.
parts.why: Caching trades origin work for another copy of data. That copy can be stale, evicted, unavailable, or flooded by many callers after one popular key expires. A design that says only “add Redis” has not explained correctness. The key and write interaction matter as much as lookup speed.
parts.example: A shortener serves 20,000 redirects per second. Use cache key link:a1b2c3d and value {destination_url, disabled_at}; the database remains authoritative. On a miss, read the row by primary key, reject a disabled link, fill the cache with a 24-hour TTL, and return 302. At a 95% hit rate, database read load falls to about 1,000 per second. When the owner changes or disables the link, commit the database update and delete that exact cache key. There is a failure window: if the process crashes after commit but before deletion, readers can see the old value until TTL. Reduce that risk with a durable invalidation event or outbox retry, and use a shorter TTL or an additional safety check when stale redirects are unacceptable. If a viral key expires while 5,000 requests arrive, request coalescing lets one caller refill it while others wait; randomized TTLs keep many keys from expiring together. If the cache times out, fall back to the database only if the database can absorb the degraded load, and protect it with limits. Negative caching of unknown codes can reduce repeated misses, but its short TTL must not hide a newly created code for long.
parts.use: Cache read-heavy, repeatedly requested data when estimates show meaningful origin relief and the product can define staleness. Prefer keys aligned with existing access paths, record hit and miss rates, and test the cache-down path. Treat invalidation as part of the corresponding write design.
parts.refuse: Do not use a cache as the only durable copy of an acknowledged write. Avoid claiming strong consistency with TTL-only expiration, caching one giant object behind a hot global key, or adding a cache before the uncached query is understood. If data is rarely reread or every value is unique, the extra copy may add cost without useful hits.

body:
Rule. Put a cache in front of a specific hot read only after defining the source-of-truth path. Name the key, value, TTL, fill policy, invalidation or refresh behavior, and acceptable staleness. Then handle misses, simultaneous expiry, and cache failure. A hit-rate estimate is useful only when it translates into reduced origin load.

Why it matters. Caching trades origin work for another copy of data. That copy can be stale, evicted, unavailable, or flooded by many callers after one popular key expires. A design that says only “add Redis” has not explained correctness. The key and write interaction matter as much as lookup speed.

Worked example. A shortener serves 20,000 redirects per second. Use cache key link:a1b2c3d and value {destination_url, disabled_at}; the database remains authoritative. On a miss, read the row by primary key, reject a disabled link, fill the cache with a 24-hour TTL, and return 302. At a 95% hit rate, database read load falls to about 1,000 per second. When the owner changes or disables the link, commit the database update and delete that exact cache key. There is a failure window: if the process crashes after commit but before deletion, readers can see the old value until TTL. Reduce that risk with a durable invalidation event or outbox retry, and use a shorter TTL or an additional safety check when stale redirects are unacceptable. If a viral key expires while 5,000 requests arrive, request coalescing lets one caller refill it while others wait; randomized TTLs keep many keys from expiring together. If the cache times out, fall back to the database only if the database can absorb the degraded load, and protect it with limits. Negative caching of unknown codes can reduce repeated misses, but its short TTL must not hide a newly created code for long.

[[diagram:cache-aside]]

When to use. Cache read-heavy, repeatedly requested data when estimates show meaningful origin relief and the product can define staleness. Prefer keys aligned with existing access paths, record hit and miss rates, and test the cache-down path. Treat invalidation as part of the corresponding write design.

When to refuse. Do not use a cache as the only durable copy of an acknowledged write. Avoid claiming strong consistency with TTL-only expiration, caching one giant object behind a hot global key, or adding a cache before the uncached query is understood. If data is rarely reread or every value is unique, the extra copy may add cost without useful hits.
